opus-5.5.text:
Well, the ecosystem has spent years optimizing for one way of generating text. Almost every serving stack in production today, whether vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, or the in-house systems at the big labs, assumes autoregressive generation: one token at a time, left to right. Every layer of that stack is built around that assumption.

Take the KV cache. In an autoregressive model, once you've computed attention keys and values for a token, they never change, so you cache them and reuse them on every subsequent step. A lot of serving engineering, like paged attention, prefix caching, and memory management, is really about managing that cache well. With a diffusion language model, you generate a whole block of tokens in parallel and refine it over several denoising steps, often with bidirectional attention within the block. The tokens you're working on change from step to step, so the standard caching story doesn't carry over directly. You have to rethink what you cache, when it's valid, and how to approximate it without losing quality.

Batching and scheduling are similar. Continuous batching is designed around requests that each emit one token per forward pass. With diffusion, the unit of work is different. You have a number of refinement steps over a chunk of tokens, and you might want to adapt how many steps you take depending on how hard the content is. So the scheduler has to reason about a different kind of workload.

Then there are the kernels. A lot of low-level optimization targets the memory-bound regime of autoregressive decoding, where you load all the weights to produce a single token. Diffusion models are much more compute-bound, because you're processing many tokens per forward pass. That's actually the whole point. It's why we can use GPUs far more efficiently and get much higher throughput and lower latency. But to realize that advantage, you need kernels and inference engines tuned for that regime, not ones inherited from the autoregressive world.

So when we started building these models, the modeling side was only half the battle. You can have a model that is, in principle, five or ten times faster, but if you drop it into infrastructure built for autoregressive models, you leave most of that speed on the table. We had to build a lot of the serving stack ourselves. Going forward, I think one of the most important things for adoption is that the open-source tooling catches up, so diffusion models become as easy to deploy as standard LLMs.

r001.rationale: The response describes serving infrastructure as a barrier to adoption, but does not say that this is why diffusion language models have few production providers.

r002.rationale: It explains that autoregressive serving stacks rely on assumptions diffusion models violate, says key components do not carry over directly, and notes that a tuned serving stack had to be built.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing to keep in mind is that essentially the entire inference stack that exists today has been built around autoregressive models. Everything from the low-level kernels to the serving frameworks like vLLM or TensorRT-LLM, to the way people think about batching and scheduling requests, it all assumes that you're generating one token at a time, left to right, and that you have a KV cache that you can incrementally extend. That's a very specific set of assumptions, and the whole industry has spent years optimizing around them.

Diffusion language models break those assumptions. In our case, with Mercury, you're generating many tokens in parallel, you're refining a whole block of text over a sequence of denoising steps rather than appending one token at a time. So the computational pattern is fundamentally different. The batching logic is different, the memory access patterns are different, the way you'd want to cache intermediate computation is different. You can't just drop a diffusion model into an existing serving engine and expect it to be fast. If you do that naively, you actually lose a lot of the speed advantage that the model architecture gives you in principle.

So we found ourselves in a position where we essentially had to build a lot of this from scratch. The kernels, the scheduler, how you handle continuous batching when requests have different lengths and are at different stages of the denoising process, how you expose a streaming-like experience to the user when you're not producing tokens strictly sequentially. These are all open engineering problems, and there's no mature open-source ecosystem to lean on the way there is for autoregressive models.

And I think that's actually a general lesson about new architectures. The algorithmic idea is maybe twenty percent of the work. The other eighty percent is making it run efficiently on real hardware, at scale, with the latency and reliability guarantees that enterprise customers expect. The autoregressive paradigm has had a huge head start on that side, and closing that gap is honestly where a lot of our effort goes.

r001.rationale: The response describes immature serving infrastructure and engineering challenges, but does not say these explain why diffusion language models have few production providers.

r002.rationale: It says existing serving engines assume autoregressive generation and that you cannot drop a diffusion model into one and expect it to be fast.

astra-6.text:
A lot of the infrastructure we have for serving language models is built around autoregressive generation. The assumption is that you generate one token at a time, and the whole stack—from KV caching to batching and scheduling requests—is optimized for that pattern.

Diffusion language models have a different computational pattern. You’re refining many tokens in parallel over several steps. That creates opportunities for speedups, but you can’t necessarily take an existing serving system, plug in a diffusion model, and expect to get those benefits automatically.

So there’s a gap between showing that a model can generate efficiently in an experiment and making it efficient under real production workloads, with different sequence lengths, concurrent requests, and latency constraints. I see that as an engineering challenge: we need serving infrastructure that takes advantage of how these models actually generate text.

r001.rationale: It describes serving infrastructure as an engineering challenge for production, but does not state that this explains why diffusion language models have few production providers.

r002.rationale: It says existing systems cannot automatically deliver diffusion models’ efficiency benefits; it does not say those systems cannot serve diffusion language models directly.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of the serving infrastructure we have today has been optimized for autoregressive models. You generate one token at a time, you cache the previous computation, and you have very sophisticated systems for batching requests and keeping the GPUs busy. Diffusion models have a different computational pattern: you’re updating many tokens in parallel over several refinement steps. So you can’t necessarily take an existing serving stack and expect to get the full benefit of that parallelism.

That’s both a challenge and an opportunity. There’s potential to generate text much faster, but realizing that in production means figuring out batching, memory management, and how to schedule those refinement steps efficiently. The model is one part of the story; the system around it has to be designed to take advantage of how it generates.

r001.rationale: It describes serving infrastructure as a challenge to production deployment, but does not say this is why diffusion language models have few production providers.

r002.rationale: It says existing stacks may not capture diffusion’s full parallelism, but does not state that autoregressive serving engines cannot directly serve diffusion models.
